qs.q: A molecular biology student analyzing the human genome sequence calculates the approximate fraction of total genomic DNA that actually encodes functional proteins. Which percentage range is accurate?
qs.e: Only about one to two percent of the human genome directly encodes functional protein sequences.

qs.q: A molecular biology instructor highlights structural differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic protein-coding sequences. Which feature is uniquely characteristic of typical prokaryotic genes?
qs.e: Prokaryotic genes are frequently organized into polycistronic operons transcribed into a single mRNA molecule.

qs.q: A molecular biology team analyzes the minimal functional segment of DNA that dictates the synthesis of one single polypeptide chain or enzyme. What historical term is used for this specific genetic unit?
qs.e: A cistron represents the genetic unit corresponding to a single gene encoding a polypeptide chain.

qs.q: A molecular biology researcher is studying a DNA sample exhibiting a left-handed helix with a zig-zag appearance and twelve base pairs per turn. Which conformation is this?
qs.e: Z-DNA forms a distinct left-handed double helix characterized by a zig-zag sugar-phosphate backbone.

qs.q: A molecular biology student examines nucleotide structure. Which chemical bond links the phosphate group of one nucleotide to the sugar residue of another in a nucleic acid strand?
qs.e: Phosphodiester bonds link the 3'-carbon of one sugar to the 5'-carbon of the next via a phosphate group.

qs.q: A molecular biology student compares prokaryotic and eukaryotic gene regulation and examines the classic operon model. Who originally proposed this operon concept for prokaryotic control?
o: Watson and Crick with DNA structure.
Beadle and Tatum with metabolic mutants.
Mendel and Bateson with pea plant crosses.
Jacob and Monod with bacterial induction.
qs.e: François Jacob and Jacques Monod proposed the operon model to explain transcriptional gene regulation in prokaryotes.

qs.q: A molecular biology student attempts to perform PCR without adding magnesium chloride to the master mix. Following thermal cycling, agarose gel electrophoresis reveals zero amplification products. Why did the omission of this divalent cation halt the reaction?
o: The DNA primers could not form stable hydrogen bonds with templates
The catalytic activity of the thermostable DNA polymerase was abolished
The thermal denaturation of the double-stranded DNA was completely blocked
The individual dNTP precursors precipitated out of the aqueous solution
The pH of the reaction buffer shifted outside the stable enzymatic range
qs.e: Divalent magnesium ions act as essential cofactors required for the catalytic function of all DNA polymerases.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Molecular Biology Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A molecular biology student is setting up a PCR amplification. The protocol specifies a final extension step at seventy-two degrees Celsius for ten minutes after the thermal cycling is complete. What is the primary biochemical purpose of this final step?
o: Allows remaining primers to anneal to newly formed strands.
Irreversibly denatures the thermostable polymerase enzyme.
Guarantees full extension of all partially synthesized strands.
Causes amplified double‑stranded DNA to precipitate out.
Enables exonuclease digestion of residual single‑stranded primers.
qs.e: A final prolonged extension step ensures that all single-stranded PCR products are fully completed and adenylated by the polymerase.

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Molecular biology studies DNA, RNA and proteins to explain how cells store, copy and use genetic information. Clinicians use this knowledge to interpret genetic tests, understand pathogen mechanisms and guide targeted therapies.

sections.p: Molecular biology examines the flow of genetic information (DNA → RNA → protein) and how alterations cause disease.
b: Central dogma: DNA transcribed to RNA, translated to protein
Key molecules: DNA, mRNA, tRNA, ribosomes, polymerases

sections.p: Transcription copies a gene into messenger RNA; translation reads mRNA codons to assemble a protein chain.
b: RNA polymerase binds promoter → initiates transcription
Ribosome reads codons → tRNA delivers amino acids
Post‑translational modifications fine‑tune protein function

sections.p: Gene expression is controlled at multiple levels to match cellular needs and external signals.
b: Promoter/enhancer binding by transcription factors
RNA splicing, stability, and microRNA silencing
Feedback inhibition of enzymes

sections.p: Mutations, epigenetic changes or viral integration disrupt normal protein production, leading to disease.
b: Point mutations → sickle‑cell disease, thalassaemia
Gene deletions/duplications → Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Oncogenic viruses (HPV, EBV) insert oncogenes
Epigenetic silencing → tumor suppressor loss

sections.p: Molecular tests diagnose inherited disorders, identify infectious agents, and select targeted cancer therapies.
b: PCR for TB, HIV, malaria parasites
BRCA1/2 sequencing for breast‑cancer risk
CFTR mutation panel for cystic fibrosis
NGS panels for rare metabolic diseases

t.b: Confirms active TB when sputum smear is negative; a positive result guides anti‑TB therapy
Distinguishes sickle‑cell disease from other hemoglobinopathies; informs transfusion and hydroxyurea decisions
Identifies pathogenic variants; positive result triggers surveillance or prophylactic surgery

sections.p: Focus on the flow of genetic information, common mutation types, and the clinical use of molecular diagnostics.
b: Remember the Hershey‑Chase experiment proved DNA is the genetic material
Differentiate between loss‑of‑function and gain‑of‑function mutations
Know which test answers which clinical question (e.g., PCR = presence of pathogen DNA)

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly progressive neurological decline with a known metabolic gene defect
Severe anemia in a child with suspected sickle‑cell disease
Unexplained fever in an immunocompromised patient with negative cultures – consider viral PCR

faq.q: Why do we test for viral DNA instead of antibodies in acute infection?
faq.a: DNA appears earlier than antibodies, allowing earlier diagnosis and treatment.

faq.q: What is the clinical impact of a silent mutation?
faq.a: Often no effect, but it can alter splicing or regulatory sites, causing disease.

faq.q: How does epigenetic silencing contribute to cancer?
faq.a: Methylation of tumor‑suppressor promoters shuts down their expression, promoting uncontrolled growth.

exam: Explain the steps of the central dogma and give one clinical example for each step.
Describe how PCR is used to diagnose tuberculosis and what a positive result means.
List three types of genetic mutations and the diseases most commonly associated with each.
